61.quote_or_event: “And this boy, after having passed his childhood, and, with just ripened intellect, having reached the state of youth, will repeat, fully understand, and well retain (in his mind) the four Vedas … and in many other brahmanical [and monastic] sciences besides.”
61.explanation: Interpreting Devânandâ's fourteen dreams, her husband foretells that the child she carries will grow into a youth of ripened intellect who masters every branch of learning; the prophecy is the reason the dreams are called fortunate.
61.tie_back: Like Valluvar, the Kalpa Sutra counts it the highest blessing of a pregnancy that the child will become one who knows what is worth knowing.
61.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Mahâvîra §§9–10 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)
61._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; it is a prophecy about one particular child (the future Mahâvîra) rather than a general maxim, and the learning named is Vedic, so the fit is partial.

62.quote_or_event: “The study of the Vêdas will not save you; the feeding of Brâhmanas will lead you from darkness to darkness, and the birth of sons will not save you. Who will assent to what you said?”
62.explanation: When their Brahmin father argues that there is no better world for men without sons, the two sons of Bhrigu reply that sons cannot save anyone; only one's own conduct under the Law frees the soul.
62.tie_back: Jainism agrees with Valluvar that the seven births matter, but it rejects the idea that a child's goodness can shield a parent's soul: in Jain doctrine each soul bears its own karma, which is the opposite of what this kural claims.
62.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 14.8 and 14.12 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)
62._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; included as an honest counterpoint, because Jain karma theory denies that a child's merit can protect a parent across births.

63.quote_or_event: “As long as a tree retains its branches, it is really a tree; when they are lopped off, it is called a trunk. As a bird without its wings, as a king in battle without his followers, as a merchant on a boat without his goods, even so am I without my sons.”
63.explanation: The priest Bhrigu, about to follow his renouncing sons into the order, says that a man's sons are his branches, wings, retinue and cargo, and without them he is diminished.
63.tie_back: Bhrigu's merchant 'without his goods' makes the same point as the kural's opening line, that one's children are one's true wealth.
63._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; it matches the first line (children as wealth) but not the second (children's wealth coming from their own deeds), and in the lecture the sentiment is a step toward renunciation.

64.quote_or_event: On the twelfth day after Mahâvîra's birth his parents prepared plenty of food, drink, spices and sweetmeats, invited friends, relatives and the Jñâtrika Kshatriyas, and sat down with them to eat, taste and share the meal before announcing the child's name, Vardhamâna.
64.explanation: The Kalpa Sutra makes a shared family meal the centre of the celebration of a newborn son.
64.tie_back: The scene links food and the joy of a child, but nothing in it matches Valluvar's image of a meal made sweeter than nectar by a small child's hands.
64.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Mahâvîra §§104–107 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)
64._accuracy_note: Paraphrased from the verified Jacobi text. No Jain source found treats a child's touch on food as a delight; this is a next-best thematic neighbour only.

65.quote_or_event: “Feeling her child quivering, trembling, moving, and stirring, the Kshatriyânî Trisalâ--glad, pleased, and joyful, &c.--spoke thus: ‘No, forsooth, the fruit of my womb has not been taken from me, it has not died, it is not fallen, it is not lost. Formerly it did not move, but now it does move.’”
65.explanation: After the unborn Mahâvîra lay still out of compassion for his mother and she feared him dead, he stirred slightly, and her grief turned to joy at the feel of her child moving.
65.tie_back: Trisalâ's delight at simply feeling her child is a scriptural instance of what this kural says: the touch of one's child is the body's greatest pleasure.
65.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Mahâvîra §§92–94 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)
65._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; it is touch felt in the womb rather than the touch of a born child, and hearing (the kural's second half) is not addressed. The resolve at the end of §94 was used for Kural 41; this is a different sentence.

66.quote_or_event: When Trisalâ believed her unborn child had died, ‘in the palace of king Siddhârtha the music of drums and stringed instruments, the clapping of hands, the dramatical performances, and the amusements of the people ceased, and mournful dejection reigned there.’
66.explanation: Once the child seemed lost, the royal musicians and players fell silent, because without the child their music had nothing to celebrate.
66.tie_back: Valluvar ranks a child's prattle above flute and lute, and here music loses all its sweetness when the child seems gone, which places the child above the instruments.
66.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Mahâvîra §92 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)
66._accuracy_note: The quoted clause is verbatim from Jacobi, but the entry is marked as a paraphrased event because it frames a narrative. It has nothing on a child's speech, so it is a partial, next-best match.

67.quote_or_event: “He studied the seventy-two arts, and acquired knowledge of the world; he was in the bloom of youth, and had a fine figure and good looks.”
67.explanation: Samudrapâla, son of the Jain layman Pâlita, was raised in his father's house to master the seventy-two arts before he went on to renounce the world and reach liberation.
67.tie_back: A devout Jain father seeing his son fully educated in all the recognised arts is close to Valluvar's idea of a father's duty to make his son pre-eminent among the learned.
67._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; the text says the son studied in his father's house but does not explicitly credit the father or mention a learned assembly, so the fit is partial.

68.quote_or_event: “In this way all (these) professors of the Law gradually obtained enlightenment … The king and the queen, the Brahmanical Purôhita, his wife, and his sons, they all reached perfection.”
68.explanation: Bhrigu's two sons, wiser than their Vedic father, first convert him and their mother, and through that example the king and queen of Ishukâra are converted too, so all six reach liberation.
68.tie_back: Valluvar says children wiser than their parents delight the whole world. In this Jain story the sons' greater wisdom spreads beyond the family to the king and queen and frees them all.
68.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 14.6–7 and 14.51–53 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)
68._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a strong narrative fit. Other verses of this lecture (14.24–28, 14.40) were used for Kurals 36 and 38.

69.quote_or_event: “Then the eye-disease was washed away like mud by Lady Marudevī’s copious tears of joy, when she heard this. She saw her son’s Tirthakṛt-splendor accompanied by the supernatural powers, and from joy at the sight of that, her absorption-in-that took place.”
69.explanation: Marudevî had wept herself nearly blind with grief for her son Rishabha, the first Tîrthankara, who had become a wandering ascetic; when Bharata told her of her son's glory, her tears of joy healed her eyes and she attained omniscience and liberation then and there.
69.tie_back: A mother whose joy on hearing her son praised exceeds anything she felt before is exactly this kural's picture, and the Jain account makes that joy powerful enough to liberate her.
69.source: Hemacandra, Trishashtishalakapurushacharitra, Book I (Âdîshvaracharitra), ch. III, part 12, 'Marudevî's omniscience and death' (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS, 1931)
69._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org; a close match, although the son is praised as a Jina rather than simply as a man of worth (cāṉṟōṉ).

70.quote_or_event: Mahâvîra stayed in his parents' house until they died, then fulfilled his promise and renounced the world, and the Laukântika gods hailed him: ‘Victory, victory to thee, gladdener of the world! … Establish the religion of the law which benefits all living beings in the whole universe!’
70.explanation: The son kept his vow not to leave home during his parents' lifetime, and his later life drew the praise of gods and men.
70.tie_back: The kural says a son repays his father by living so that others marvel at the father who produced him; Mahâvîra's dutiful wait and the praise that followed match this only loosely.
70.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Mahâvîra §§110–111 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)
70._accuracy_note: The hymn wording is verbatim from Jacobi, but the entry is a paraphrased event. The praise is for Mahâvîra himself, not for his father, so the fit is partial; the related vow of §94 was used for Kural 41.
